justification: Key B is the netting comparison verbatim ('more than the trap has held in fifteen years'), and fifteen springs is the whole life of the book. A dies on 'Since the pass opened in 2011 the trap has been emptied most mornings of the run, the counts written into a hardbacked book' - the record begins in 2011, and 1931 is only when the mill stopped. C dies because the passage volunteers exactly one limitation of the book, 'the book counts only what went through the box', and it is not misidentification; 'The first nine springs are in one hand, the rest in three others' reports who wrote, not what was written, and chub and dace stand as separate lines with no note of doubt. D dies on that same clause - four hands, not one. Note C is the only hedged option in the set and it is a distractor, so hedge-hunting is punished rather than rewarded.

Key D is arithmetic: 39 entered, twelve came out at the top. A dies on 'Of the eleven that entered above ten degrees, seven got out; of the twenty-eight that entered colder, five did' - 64 per cent against 18 per cent; 'suggestive and no more' hedges the causal claim, not the gap in rates. B dies on 'She tagged 212 dace' set against 'Of 74 tagged'. C dies on the passage's actual explanation being build and behaviour - 'deep through the body and carries a dorsal fin like a sail, and it does not leave the water' - with strength set aside for dace earlier; 'deep through the body' is the only size-flavoured phrase and C's fatal half is 'rather than their build'. Internal arithmetic checks out (11+28=39 entrants, 7+5=12 through), so the key cannot be knocked over on the numbers.

Key A is Kelsingham's stated reason plus the attraction-flow sentence ('Four metres out from the mouth there is nothing of that quarter left to follow'). B dies on 'thinks strength has little to do with it' and 'The dace aren't beaten by the ladder', with the stem scoped to her account, and on five of the nine entrants reaching the top. C dies on absence of any seasonal opening - the pass is a fixed chute and 'opened in 2011' means commissioned - and on '174 of them had been read at the weir' with nine going in. D is the best-built near-miss because 'They move up in loose shoals along the margins' is verbatim, but it dies on Kelsingham's own causal statement, 'They don't find it, and they don't find it because they don't come up that side of the river': the shoaling does its work by putting the fish on the wrong margin, not by making them refuse a narrow slot, and nine dace did enter singly.

Key C is what the final contrast implies: one orifice packed, 'The other, three walls further up, came through the same water clear'. A dies on 'the same water', which makes the spate a shared constant rather than the differentiator, and on 'in three of those fifteen winters it came over the crest deep enough to drown the weir out' - much bigger water is routine here, so nothing grounds 'heavier than the river usually brings'; A also answers about the spate rather than about the orifices the stem asks after. B is right in the world - cutting orifices really does draw discharge off the notches above - but dies on the stated purpose, 'so a fish could go through a wall instead of over it'. D is the nearest miss in the unit: 'instead of over it' describes the fish's route past a wall, not the abolition of the notch; the walls were 'cut with' orifices, an addition; only two of the nine were cut, so nothing systemic is replaced; and 'What has been tried is smaller' frames them as a minor add-on. The stem asks what is implied, and D garbles something explicit rather than answering it.

Key D names the article's structure: trout up 'without appearing to try', dace and grayling mostly not, and two different reasons - finding the entrance versus climbing the notches. A dies on scope - the temperature split is one sub-finding Kelsingham calls 'suggestive and no more', and it touches neither dace nor trout. B is the runner-up and the one worth naming: the book of counts does open the piece, but the article's engine is the tagging study across three of five paragraphs, and the counts are explicitly shown to be an incomplete instrument ('the book counts only what went through the box', three drowned-out winters), so they pose the puzzle rather than 'support the case'; the piece also makes no normative claim about how passes should be judged. C dies on 'The river below it is thick with dace; one afternoon's netting last May took four hundred-odd of them' - no decline, and populations above the weir are never mentioned.

Key D: 'fetch' is the one verb in the set that takes the goods as subject for the price they realise, and it is the standard BrE verb for it. A 'earned' needs an animate earner or a beneficiary object ('earned her two pounds'); with the jacket as bare subject it reads as the jacket acquiring money. B 'gained' fails the same way and more plainly - gain is acquisition for oneself. C 'returned' takes an investment or a sale as subject, not the goods, and its give-back sense actively misleads at a jumble sale. The set is a clean argument-structure gap: all three distractors misassign the subject role, so none is collocationally live.

Key C: 'worth' takes the -ing form, so 'worth keeping open' is the only grammatical fill. A 'keep' and B 'kept' are ungrammatical after 'worth'. D 'to keep' is the classic L1-transfer trap and is likewise ungrammatical - 'worth to keep' is not available in standard English. A pure form gap with a unique answer; low discrimination by design, but no distractor survives.

Key B: 'nothing has a price after that' and 'They're doing us a favour' make it a giveaway, and the frame 'moves from a sale to a ___' requires something that is not selling. A 'clearance' dies on that requirement twice over - a clearance is a sale, and it implies reduced prices where the passage says there are none. C 'markdown' dies on the same span and is in any case a price reduction, not an event type that contrasts with a sale. D 'liquidation' dies on 'nothing has a price after that' and on register - insolvency vocabulary for a village hall. All three distractors keep prices in play; only the key removes them.

Key B: the paragraph's stated sorting principle is time - boxes 'that arrive after two', 'sorted by arrival time at least as much as by taste' - so short exposure, not rejection, is the explanation. A 'amply' is not a collocation with 'offered' and would reverse the argument. C is the nearest miss - 'About a dozen people are left' makes a sparse-audience reading tempting - but 'thinly' makes the offering itself sparse rather than short, which is incoherent for one coat, and it does not track the arrival-time argument the sentence is built on. D 'openly' is the live collocation of the three and is exactly the right kind of trap: idiomatic but logically inert, since openness would not explain an item going unsold.

Key A: 'The pattern is not a law' plus the named exceptions, then a reassertion - 'Still' is the concessive-reversal the paragraph needs. B 'Granted' is the subtlest distractor but runs backwards: the concession has already been spent on the exceptions, this clause reasserts the pattern, and 'Granted' would require a following 'but' that the sentence does not have. C 'Therefore' would make the exceptions the cause of her accuracy. D 'Occasionally' is contradicted by 'be wrong about one in four', a stable three-in-four success rate rather than an intermittent one.

Key C is verbatim: 'Where the glue went in, the sheet's gone like greased paper; you can read the back through it'. A dies on the em-dash clause 'The rubber in it has oxidised - that's the brown' - the brown is oxidised rubber, while the plasticiser is what 'has soaked into the paper'; A swaps the two and adds an unstated timing claim. B is exactly reversed and dies on two clauses: 'A mend from last year I warm, and the film lifts' against 'One like this, heat won't shift. The glue's gone hard, so it's solvent'. D dies on the explicit refusal that closes the quote: 'The brown that's in the fibres I can lighten. I don't promise to take it out'. All four options are equally absolute and equal in length, so there is no hedge or length cue on the key.

Key A is a real inference, not a restatement: the only thing that ended a continuation was a claim on the slate, 'a volume so claimed came in on the fourteenth day', and 39 of the travels' 41 loans came in on that day - so a reader was waiting; the sermons (continued seven times of nine) supply the internal control. B dies on 'nothing was charged before the twenty-ninth day, when a penny a day began' - a second fortnight is days 15 to 28 and free. C is true of many book societies of the period and false of this one: 'Fifty-three subscribers paid a guinea a year, and three of them chose what was bought'. D dies on 'Eleven of the fifty-three paid their guinea in each of the nine years and carried nothing home' - they never stopped paying. Arithmetic is internally consistent (41 = 39 + 2; 9 = 7 + 2).

Key C is stated outright: “buföringen dit bestämdes på byastämman: djuren fick inte gå upp innan löven var utslagna”. A is the best-built distractor because hay is a load-bearing theme (“en ko som betade på hemängen i juli åt upp det hö hon skulle leva på i februari”), but that logic explains why the animals left, not when, and the stem asks for the timing. B dies because “lönen gjordes upp i maj, innan buföringen” fixes an order of events, not a cause; what decided it is named explicitly. D is true in the world - snowmelt governs when mountain pasture is usable - but snow and ice appear nowhere in the text, which names leaf-out instead. A sound pair: one world-knowledge option and one theme option, both killed by the same sentence.

Key D is the text's own contrast: “två kvinnor på samma vall lockade därför inte lika” against “Dess signaler var få och bestämda”. A is the sharpest trap, since kulning's reputation for carrying argues for it, but the passage anticipates the intuition and refutes it: “De hördes till Klintbodarna och en stilla kväll ända ned till byn, längre än något rop bar”. B dies on “med den lockades djuren hem om kvällen” - the calls are evening work, not dawn - and on the fog use carrying no time of day. C misplaces both of its hooks: it is the animals that learn, up on the vall (“lära djuren att känna igen just hennes rop”), and Klintbodarna is where the horn was heard, not where signals were taught.

Key A is verbatim: “lönen gjordes upp i maj, innan buföringen: till större delen varor ... och en mindre summa pengar”. B dies on that same sentence - a wage settled in May cannot vary with August's cheeses - and on the reward for a well-kept vall being a different one (“kunde välja gård nästa år”). C is the nearest miss: “betalades ut på hösten” invites a causal gloss, but the text gives a date, not a condition; the wage was fixed in advance, mostly in goods, and no sale of the fäbod produce is described anywhere before the dairy of 1904. D is a clever trap for a reader who knows the period - the annual tjänsteår was the norm and “mikaelitiden” baits it - but it dies on “Fäbodfolket lejdes för en sommar i taget”.

Key B is the author's own controlling idea, stated twice: “allt som skulle bäras hem måste först göras hållbart” and “avståndet betydde litet så länge varan tålde att vänta. Nu satte avståndet i stället priset”; it covers paragraphs 1, 4, 5, 6, 7 and 8. A dies on scope - the vallkullor hold one paragraph of nine, and neither the reason for the system, nor its collapse, nor Pilhammar, nor what survives would fall under such a heading. C is the strongest near-miss in the batch, since paragraphs 6-7 are exactly the turn-of-century transformation, but the heading is simultaneously too wide (“jordbruket” never names the fäbod) and too narrow (the first five paragraphs go unaccounted for), and the transformation is the answer to a question the text sets up rather than its subject. D dies on scope - the overgrowth is two sentences in paragraph 8.

Key D is the subtraction 74 minus 58: “Sjuttiofyra sökte plats till den marknaden, och alla femtioåtta stånd var upptagna när den öppnade”. A dies on “Den som stod på torget året innan får stå där igen” and on pitch 1 standing in Runesson's name “längre än platskartan går tillbaka” - tenure, not a lottery. B dies on “blev lediga” (fell vacant, not were added) and on “Torget rymmer femtioåtta stånd och fler får inte plats”. C is a straight inversion of the same tenure rule. Observation with no consequence for the distractors: the subtraction assumes the 74 are the whole applicant pool; a reader who takes renewal to be automatic could instead set 74 against the four vacancies and get 70. The adjacent clause “alla femtioåtta stånd var upptagna” is placed precisely to license the subtraction and would be idle on the other reading, and no option offers the alternative figure - so no second correct answer arises.

Key A is the stated thesis plus the concession: “Flytta hela marknaden, båda dagarna, från och med nästa höst” and “De första åren blir sämre ... jag tänker inte påstå att det ordnar sig av sig självt”. B is the most attractive, since the author herself says “Det svaret har jag inte” about the two-day problem, but “båda dagarna” sits in the imperative sentence exactly to close that escape. C is half true - “De trettionio har två skäl, och båda håller” - but is killed by “Jag var en av de tolv” and by the closing imperative; conceding an argument is not adopting the position. D dies on “Ett provår vill jag ändå inte ha ... Att stå ett år på fältet och sedan flytta tillbaka lär ingen någonting”. An unusually well-built set: the text plants each temptation and then names its own refusal of it.

Key A is the text's explicit criterion: “gick inte efter hur nära man stod varandra, utan efter vad besöket gällde” and “De kom i ärenden som rörde hushållet”. B dies on “Grannar och släkt satt i köket, oavsett hur långt de hade rest”. C dies on “Sköterskan var oanmäld varannan gång och visades in ändå”. D is the intuitive reading - the finrum is the house's best room - but it is killed both by the criterion sentence and by who was let in: “karlen som skulle värdera skogen”, a hired valuer no household would rank highest, while the neighbour Lars Uddén is left standing in the farstu with his cap in his hand.

Key C follows from “Sen bar far ut den i köket, för där gick spisen ändå” together with “Dörren till finrummet gick igen som förut”. A is the sharpest distractor, because the paragraph order invites a chronological reading, but it is killed by the author's own closing sentence: “Hemma hos oss stod farfars kista i finrummet flera år efter att vår apparat hade burits ut” - home funerals outlasted the set's stay, so its placement cannot have followed their move to the chapel. B dies on “Samma soffgrupp står kvar hos honom”. D dies on “stod den i tre vintrar innan huset fick element, och de satt i ytterrock framför den” - the exact reverse.
